headline: A Protein Switch That Burns Fat Without Cutting Muscle
meta_description: Scientists at Weizmann Institute discover disabling a protein called MTCH2 makes cells burn more fat while preserving lean muscle—a promising new obesity treat…
summary_short: Researchers found that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and blocks new fat cells from forming, offering hope for obesity treatment.
body:
Scientists at the Weizmann Institute of Science have discovered a protein called MTCH2—nicknamed "Mitch"—that acts as a metabolic switch, controlling whether cells burn fat or store it. When researchers disabled this protein in laboratory experiments, human cells began consuming more fuel, including fats and carbohydrates, while also preventing immature cells from developing into fat cells. The findings, published in The EMBO Journal in January 2025, suggest a fundamentally different path to treating obesity: not by suppressing appetite, but by changing how the body's cells actually use energy.

Earlier mouse studies had hinted at Mitch's power. When scientists removed the protein from muscle tissue in genetically modified mice, the animals showed increased metabolic activity, resisted diet-related obesity, and developed muscle fibers with greater capacity for using oxygen—improving their endurance and heart function. The breakthrough matters because current weight-loss medications, while effective, have a hidden cost: a 2026 analysis of 20 clinical trials involving 15,782 participants found that 25 to 39 percent of weight lost came from lean muscle mass rather than fat alone.

The mechanism behind Mitch's influence lies in mitochondria, the cellular powerhouses that convert food into usable energy. Researchers found that Mitch controls mitochondrial fusion—the process where separate mitochondria merge into larger, interconnected networks. Without this protein, the mitochondrial network fragments, forcing cells to operate in a more energy-intensive state and consume more fuel. For people struggling with weight, the implications are striking: a treatment that burns fat while preserving muscle could offer the best of both worlds—genuine fat loss without sacrificing the strength and health that muscle provides.
quick_facts: Weizmann Institute scientists identified protein MTCH2, nicknamed 'Mitch'
Disabling Mitch makes cells burn more fat and blocks new fat cell formation
Findings published in The EMBO Journal in January 2025
Current weight-loss drugs cause 25–39% of weight loss to come from muscle
Mitch controls mitochondrial fusion, forcing cells to consume more fuel
